Newly hatched Western jackdaw chicks weigh a modest 11.3 grams [Wwb = 11.3 grams], a value typical of altricial corvid nestlings that require intensive parental care during their early development. These nestlings are brooded continuously to maintain stable body temperatures, as they are poikilothermic in the first days of life. The incubation period, during which eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], lasts for approximately 18.2 days [ab = approximately 18.2 days], although field records indicate that hatching can occur anywhere from 17 to 20 days depending on microclimatic conditions and the attentiveness of the incubating adult. This rather brief incubation period is consistent with the moderate egg mass of the species and contrasts with longer incubation durations seen in larger corvids. Once the eggs hatch, the altricial young are entirely dependent on both parents for thermoregulation and food delivery. The initial body mass of 11.3 grams [Wwb = 11.3 grams] is a critical starting point for the rapid somatic growth that characterizes the nestling phase, which demands substantial provisioning effort from the breeding pair. Slight variations in this birth mass can influence early survival prospects, as heavier neonates often exhibit greater competitive ability during begging interactions with siblings. Consequently, the first days after hatching represent a vulnerable period during which thermal stability and consistent food delivery are essential for successful development.

Under the typical internal body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that active adult Western jackdaws maintain, their fledglings achieve sustained flight at approximately 35 days since birth [tx = approximately 35 days since birth]. This developmental milestone marks the transition from a sedentary nestling to a mobile juvenile capable of leaving the nest cavity. The fledging period is relatively brief compared to larger corvids such as carrion crows, reflecting the jackdaw's smaller adult body size and a life history strategy that prioritizes earlier independence. During the weeks preceding fledging, the downy chicks undergo rapid feather growth and significant mass gain as they prepare for their first flight. The parents continue to provision the fledglings extensively even after nest departure, as the young birds are still inept at foraging for themselves. This post-fledging care period is crucial for honing flight skills and learning to recognize edible prey items. Predation risk remains high during this phase, as inexperienced fledglings are less vigilant and more conspicuous to avian predators. The timing of fledging at 35 days since birth [tx = 35 days since birth] is thus a compromise between the benefits of early dispersal from the crowded nest and the need for sufficient neuromuscular development to ensure adequate escape performance against predators at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

The same core body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that supports fledging also governs the onset of reproductive maturity in Western jackdaws. Puberty, defined by the maturation of gonadal tissues and the initiation of gametogenesis, occurs at approximately 105 days since birth [tp = approximately 105 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturity is a hallmark of the species' moderately fast life history pace compared to larger, longer-lived corvids like ravens. However, the age at first successful reproduction, often termed the time since birth at first brood, is considerably more delayed at around 730 days since birth [tR = around 730 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This two-year delay between puberty and actual breeding is ecologically meaningful: young birds typically spend their first potential breeding season as non-breeding helpers or floater individuals, gaining valuable experience in foraging, territory defense, and social bonding before attempting to raise their own offspring. This deferred reproduction reflects the challenges of securing a high-quality nest cavity in competitive urban or woodland environments. The gap of approximately 625 days between gonadal maturity and first successful reproduction underscores the importance of social structure and resource acquisition in shaping the jackdaw's reproductive schedule, a pattern observed in many cooperatively breeding corvid species.

Adult body mass in Western jackdaws reaches an ultimate wet weight of approximately 260 grams [Wwi = approximately 260 grams], a value that positions the species as a medium-sized member of the Corvus genus. This asymptotic mass is attained gradually over the first year of life, as the young birds continue to grow even after reaching skeletal maturity. Field studies have shown that adult mass can fluctuate seasonally, with individuals storing substantial fat reserves during autumn to buffer against winter food scarcity. This body size allows jackdaws to exploit a wide range of nesting cavities inaccessible to larger corvids, including chimneys, hollow trees, and crevices in buildings. The relatively modest body mass also facilitates efficient flight maneuvers, a necessity for avoiding predators and competing with more aggressive corvid species at feeding sites. The ultimate wet weight therefore represents an adaptive compromise between the energetic demands of flight and the advantages of larger body size in social dominance hierarchies.
